title: Spectrum
tagline: How white light splits and recombines, the order of the electromagnetic spectrum, and why the sky is blue and the sunset is red.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ICSE Class X Physics syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). Every wavelength, frequency and speed in this chapter was independently recomputed using the speed of light in a vacuum taken as 300000000 metres per second. No board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

overview.intro: White light is not a single colour but a mixture, and the prism is the classic device that reveals the fact by splitting it into a band of colours. This chapter explains dispersion through the way refractive index varies with wavelength, sets out the visible band in its familiar order, and shows that the colours can be recombined back into white. It then places visible light in its context within the electromagnetic spectrum, running from radio waves to gamma rays, with the properties each region is used for. The final section deals with scattering: why air molecules send blue light in every direction so the sky looks blue, why the same process leaves the setting sun red, and the two optical effects that follow from refraction in the atmosphere rather than from scattering at all.

learningOutcomes: Explain dispersion and state the order of the visible colours from most to least deviated.
List the regions of the electromagnetic spectrum in order and state a use and a hazard of each.
Explain the scattering of light and use it to account for the blue sky and the red sunset.
Distinguish scattering from atmospheric refraction and account for twinkling and the extended day.

blocks.text: When a narrow beam of white light passes through a glass prism it spreads out into a band of colours running from violet at one end to red at the other, and this spreading is called dispersion. The cause is that glass does not slow every wavelength by the same amount: its refractive index is slightly larger for shorter wavelengths, so violet light, which is slowed the most, is bent the most, while red light, slowed the least, is bent the least. Each colour therefore leaves the prism travelling in its own direction, and the eye reads that set of directions as separate colours. The order from most deviated to least is violet, indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange and red, which is the mnemonic VIBGYOR read backwards from the red end. Red light has the longest wavelength and the lowest frequency of the visible band, and it is scattered least by small particles; violet has the shortest wavelength and the highest frequency and is scattered most, although the sky appears blue rather than violet because the sun emits less violet light and our eyes are less sensitive to it. Dispersion can be reversed: bringing the colours back together with a second prism, or rotating a Newton disc of coloured sectors fast enough, produces an apparently white surface.

blocks.caption: The visible colours and how they behave
rows: Strong — why the sky looks blue
Least — why a setting sun looks red

items: Dispersion is the splitting of white light into its component colours, most neatly by a prism.
The cause is that refractive index depends on wavelength, so each colour is bent by a different amount.
Violet is bent most and red least, because violet has the shortest wavelength and the highest refractive index in glass.
The order of the spectrum from the most deviated end is violet, indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange, red.
Red light has the longest wavelength and the lowest frequency within the visible band.
A single prism disperses; a second prism placed upside down can recombine the colours into white light.
A Newton disc spins coloured sectors fast enough that the eye blends them into an apparently white disc.
A thin slit is used before the prism so that the beam is narrow enough for the colours to be seen separately.

items.text: A narrow beam of sunlight passes through a prism onto a white card and produces a clean band running red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet, with red nearest the original direction of the beam.
items.note: The red end is deviated least, so it always appears closest to where the beam would have gone without the prism.

items.text: Two identical prisms placed with their apexes in opposite directions recombine the spectrum: the first spreads the colours and the second undoes the spreading, giving white light again.
items.note: The second prism must be inverted, otherwise it disperses further instead of recombining.

blocks.text: Visible light occupies only a very narrow band of a far larger family of radiations, all of which are travelling electromagnetic waves that consist of oscillating electric and magnetic fields at right angles to each other and to the direction of travel. They are transverse waves, they need no material medium, and in a vacuum they all travel at exactly the same speed, 300000000 metres per second. Arranging them by wavelength gives the electromagnetic spectrum, and in order of decreasing wavelength it runs radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays; since speed equals wavelength times frequency, decreasing wavelength means increasing frequency and increasing energy per photon. Radio waves, with wavelengths from metres to kilometres, carry broadcasting and communication signals. Microwaves, from centimetres down to millimetres, drive radar, satellite links and microwave ovens, where they heat food by making water molecules rotate. Infrared is the radiation of warm bodies and is used for heating, thermal imaging and remote controls. Ultraviolet carries enough energy to cause sunburn, to make some minerals fluoresce, and to kill bacteria, which is why it sterilises equipment. X-rays penetrate soft tissue but not bone, so they image the skeleton and scan baggage. Gamma rays, with the shortest wavelength of all, come from radioactive nuclei and are used to treat cancer and to sterilise medical instruments, but they are also the most damaging to living tissue.

blocks.caption: The electromagnetic spectrum in order of decreasing wavelength

Heating of tissue with prolonged exposure

Very bright light can dazzle or damage the retina
Sunburn, eye damage, risk with prolonged exposure

items: All electromagnetic waves are transverse and need no material medium to travel through.
In a vacuum every region travels at 300000000 metres per second, whatever its wavelength.
Wavelength times frequency equals the speed of light, so shorter wavelength always means higher frequency.
Gamma rays have the shortest wavelength and the highest frequency; radio waves have the longest and the lowest.
X-rays and gamma rays are distinguished by origin rather than by wavelength alone: gamma rays come from the nucleus.
Microwaves heat food by making water molecules rotate rather than by carrying heat directly into the food.
Ultraviolet is used to sterilise because its photon energy is high enough to damage the DNA of microbes.
Visible light is such a narrow band that it occupies only a tiny fraction of the whole spectrum.

items.text: A microwave oven emits radiation of about 12 cm wavelength that penetrates the food and makes its water molecules rotate billions of times a second, and the resulting friction heats the food from within.
items.note: The frequency of the radiation is chosen to match a rotational absorption band of water.

items.text: A hospital radiographer stands behind a lead-lined screen while an X-ray is taken, because although the patient's dose is small the scatter that leaves the patient is itself ionising.
items.note: The hazard to the operator comes from scattered rather than primary radiation.

learn.title: Scattering, the blue sky and the red sunset

blocks.text: When light meets particles that are small compared with its wavelength, the light is absorbed and re-emitted in new directions without any change of wavelength, and this is scattering. The strength of the scattering depends very sharply on wavelength: for air molecules much smaller than the wavelength of light, the amount scattered varies inversely with the fourth power of the wavelength, so blue light with a wavelength near 450 nm is scattered roughly five times as strongly as red light near 700 nm. Sunlight entering the atmosphere therefore has its blue and violet components redirected in every direction by the air molecules, and an observer looking anywhere away from the sun sees that scattered light, which is why the sky appears blue; it looks blue rather than violet because the sun emits less violet light and the eye's response peaks nearer blue. The same process explains the setting sun. Near the horizon the sunlight travels through a much longer thickness of atmosphere, so nearly all the blue is scattered out of the direct beam on its way to the observer, and what remains is the red and orange light that is scattered least — hence a red or orange sun low in the sky. Larger particles such as dust, smoke and water droplets scatter all wavelengths more equally, which is why dusty or polluted air gives a white or hazy sky rather than a deep blue one.

blocks.caption: Scattering and its consequences
rows: Blue and violet strongly, by air molecules

Blue removed from the direct beam over a long path
Only the least-scattered long wavelengths reach the eye directly
Some blue scattered out of a short atmospheric path
A white or pale yellow sun
The path through the atmosphere is at its shortest
The particles are large compared with the wavelength
This is the Tyndall effect with particles near the wavelength of light
The beam becomes visible from the side
Large droplets scatter all colours, so no colour predominates

items: Scattering changes the direction of light without changing its wavelength.
Shorter wavelengths are scattered far more strongly than longer ones by particles smaller than the wavelength.
The blue of the sky is the blue component of sunlight scattered towards the eye by air molecules.
The sky is not violet although violet is scattered even more, because the sun emits less violet and the eye is less sensitive to it.
A sunset is red because the long atmospheric path removes the blue by scattering, leaving the least-scattered colours.
Dust, smoke and water droplets are larger than air molecules and scatter all colours similarly, giving a white haze.
The Tyndall effect is the scattering of light by particles in a colloid, which makes a beam visible from the side.
Scattering is a change of direction; it must not be confused with atmospheric refraction, which is a bending by changing speed.

items.text: A shaft of afternoon sunlight enters a dusty room through a gap in the curtains and the beam is clearly visible from the side, although in clean air it would not be, because the dust particles scatter the light out of the beam towards the eye.
items.note: Seeing the beam from the side is direct evidence of scattering, not of refraction.

items.text: The same red sun that looks fierce at sunset would look white if it were viewed from above the atmosphere, since there would be no long path of air to remove the blue by scattering.
items.note: Astronauts report a white sun from orbit, which confirms the atmospheric cause.

learn.title: Effects of the atmosphere: refraction as well as scattering

blocks.text: Not every optical effect in the sky is caused by scattering, and it is worth separating the two carefully. Atmospheric refraction arises because the density of the air, and therefore its refractive index, increases downwards from the upper atmosphere towards the ground. Light from a star entering the atmosphere at an angle passes into progressively denser air and is therefore bent continuously towards the normal, so the star's apparent position is slightly higher than its true position. Because the density of the atmosphere is always changing with temperature and with pockets of moving air, the amount of bending fluctuates, and the star's apparent position wobbles slightly from moment to moment; the brightness also varies because the amount of light reaching the eye changes, and it is this flickering in position and brightness that is the twinkling. Planets are near enough to the eye to present a small disc rather than a point, so the twinkle of many points averages out and planets generally do not twinkle visibly. The same refraction also carries the light of a sun that has already set below the horizon back into view, which extends both sunrise and sunset by a few minutes and makes the day slightly longer than the geometric rotation of the Earth would allow.

blocks.caption: Atmospheric effects compared

Density fluctuations bend the light by varying amounts
A planet presents a disc, not a point

items: Atmospheric refraction is a bending by change of speed; scattering is a change of direction by re-emission.
Stars twinkle because the atmosphere above them is in constant motion, varying the refraction moment by moment.
Planets appear as small discs, so the flicker of many points averages out and they rarely twinkle visibly.
The apparent position of a star is slightly higher than its true position because of atmospheric refraction.
Sunrise and sunset are brought forward and pushed back respectively, lengthening the day by several minutes.
Both effects must be explained separately in an answer, since one is refraction and the other is scattering.
A red sunset is a scattering effect, not a refraction effect, although refraction also extends its duration.
Dust and pollution change the appearance of the sky by adding large-particle scattering to the molecular scattering.

items.text: A star low on the horizon twinkles far more fiercely than one overhead, because its light passes through a much thicker and more turbulent layer of atmosphere before reaching the eye.
items.note: The path length through the turbulent air is what sets the amount of flicker.

items.text: An observer sees the sun's upper edge when the sun is already fractionally below the geometric horizon, which is why published sunrise and sunset times differ from those calculated purely from the Earth's rotation.
items.note: The correction is a matter of minutes, but it is real and it is refraction.

keyPoints: Dispersion is the splitting of white light into its colours by a prism, caused by the refractive index varying with wavelength.
Violet is deviated most and red least; the order from most to least deviated is VIBGYOR from violet to red.
Red light has the longest visible wavelength and is scattered least; violet has the shortest and is scattered most.
White light can be recombined by an inverted second prism or by a rapidly rotating Newton disc.
The electromagnetic spectrum in order of decreasing wavelength is radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays.
All electromagnetic waves are transverse, need no medium, and travel at 300000000 metres per second in a vacuum.
Wavelength times frequency equals the speed of light, so shorter wavelength always means higher frequency.
Scattering is the change of direction of light by particles, with shorter wavelengths scattered far more strongly.
The sky is blue because air molecules scatter blue light in all directions; a sunset is red because the long path removes blue by scattering.
Stars twinkle because of atmospheric refraction varying with the moving air, while planets, being discs, do not twinkle visibly.
examFocus: Explain dispersion by naming the cause — refractive index varies with wavelength — rather than by simply saying the prism splits the light.
When ordering the electromagnetic spectrum, quote the direction of ordering; an unordered list of regions earns little.
Sky and sunset answers must state that shorter wavelengths scatter more, and must not attribute either effect to refraction.
Twinkling must be explained as atmospheric refraction with fluctuating density, not as scattering.
Quote wavelengths in nanometres with the conversion that one nanometre is one billionth of a metre when it is used in a calculation.

questions.prompt: Which colour of white light is deviated most by a glass prism, and why?
options: Red, because it has the longest wavelength
Violet, because glass has a higher refractive index for it
Green, because it lies in the middle of the spectrum
All colours are deviated equally and only differ in colour
questions.answer: Violet, because glass has a higher refractive index for it
questions.explanation: The refractive index of glass is slightly larger for shorter wavelengths, so violet light, which has the shortest visible wavelength, is slowed the most and bent the most. Red light has the longest wavelength, meets the lowest refractive index and is bent least. The unequal bending is exactly what dispersion is.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing red because it appears at one end of the spectrum. Red is deviated least, not most, which is why it lies nearest the original beam direction.

questions.prompt: In order of decreasing wavelength, the electromagnetic spectrum runs: radio waves, ________, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, ________ and gamma rays.
questions.explanation: Listing the regions from longest to shortest wavelength gives radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays. Because the speed of every one of them in a vacuum is the same, decreasing wavelength means increasing frequency and increasing energy per photon, so gamma rays carry the most energy and radio waves the least.
questions.commonMistake: Placing microwaves between infrared and visible light. Microwaves have longer wavelengths than infrared, so they belong next to radio waves.

questions.prompt: Why does the sky appear blue rather than violet, even though violet light is scattered more strongly by air molecules?
options: Because air molecules absorb violet light completely
Because the sun emits less violet light and the human eye is less sensitive to violet than to blue
Because violet light has a longer wavelength than blue light
Because blue light is refracted more strongly in the atmosphere
questions.answer: Because the sun emits less violet light and the human eye is less sensitive to violet than to blue
questions.explanation: Violet is indeed scattered more strongly than blue, so the physics alone would predict a violet sky. Two further factors decide the actual colour: sunlight contains less violet energy than blue, and the eye's sensitivity peaks nearer blue than violet, so the mixture that reaches the eye reads as blue.
questions.commonMistake: Saying violet is absorbed by the atmosphere. It is scattered, but the combination of the solar spectrum and eye sensitivity is what sets the perceived colour.

questions.prompt: Explain why the sun appears red when it is near the horizon at sunset, and state whether this is caused by scattering or by refraction.
questions.answer: When the sun is near the horizon, its light travels through a much greater thickness of atmosphere than it does at noon. Over that long path, blue and violet light, which are the most strongly scattered wavelengths, are repeatedly redirected out of the direct beam by the air molecules, so by the time the light reaches the observer almost all the blue has been removed. What remains of the direct beam is the red and orange light, which is scattered least and therefore survives the journey, and these colours reach the eye largely undisturbed. The effect is caused by scattering rather than by refraction: it is the removal of particular wavelengths from the beam by redirection, not a bending of the light by changes of atmospheric density.
questions.explanation: The answer must identify the long path, the preferential removal of short wavelengths and the survival of the long ones, and then classify the effect correctly as scattering. Stating only that the light travels further through the atmosphere leaves out why the colour changes.
questions.commonMistake: Attributing the red sunset to atmospheric refraction. Refraction does raise the apparent position of the sun, but the red colour is a scattering effect.

questions.prompt: Describe an experiment to demonstrate the dispersion of white light by a prism, and explain why the colours appear in the order they do.
questions.answer: Allow a narrow beam of sunlight to fall on a glass prism held in a darkened room, so that only a thin pencil of light enters rather than a broad beam. A white card is placed some distance beyond the prism to receive the beam, and a continuous band of colours is seen on the card, running from red nearest the original direction of the beam to violet furthest from it. The narrow beam is essential because a wide one would cause the coloured bands to overlap and appear white. The order arises because the refractive index of glass is not the same for every wavelength: it is greatest for the shortest wavelength, so violet is slowed most and deviated most, while red has the longest wavelength, is slowed least and is deviated least. Since each colour is bent by a different amount, each leaves the prism travelling in a different direction, and the eye resolves those directions as the familiar band of colours.
questions.explanation: The apparatus must specify a narrow beam and a white screen, and the explanation must attribute the order to wavelength-dependent refractive index rather than to the prism separating colours by some other means. Identifying which end of the band is deviated most is part of the explanation.
questions.commonMistake: Forgetting to mention the narrow slit. With a wide beam the bands overlap and the spectrum is not visible.

questions.prompt: Which statement about electromagnetic waves is correct?
options: They are longitudinal and need a material medium
They are transverse, need no medium, and all travel at 300000000 m per second in a vacuum
Only visible light is transverse; the rest are longitudinal
Their speed in a vacuum depends on their wavelength
questions.answer: They are transverse, need no medium, and all travel at 300000000 m per second in a vacuum
questions.explanation: Every electromagnetic wave consists of oscillating electric and magnetic fields at right angles to each other and to the direction of travel, which makes them transverse, and they propagate through empty space without any material medium. In a vacuum they all share one speed of 300000000 metres per second, so wavelength and frequency vary together to keep that product fixed.
questions.commonMistake: Thinking that gamma rays or X-rays travel faster because they carry more energy. Their speed in a vacuum is identical to that of a radio wave.

questions.prompt: Explain what is meant by the scattering of light, state how the strength of scattering depends on wavelength, and use both facts to account for the blue sky, the red sunset and the white appearance of a dusty sky.
questions.answer: Scattering is the process in which light meeting particles much smaller than its wavelength is absorbed and re-emitted in new directions, without any change of wavelength, so the light is redirected rather than absorbed or bent. The strength of the scattering depends very strongly on wavelength: for air molecules the amount varies inversely with the fourth power of the wavelength, so a short wavelength such as blue is scattered far more strongly than a long one such as red. This accounts for the blue sky, because sunlight entering the atmosphere has its blue component redirected in every direction by the air molecules, and an observer looking away from the sun sees that scattered light coming from the whole sky. It accounts for the red sunset, because near the horizon the light traverses a much longer thickness of atmosphere, so nearly all the blue is scattered out of the direct beam and only the least-scattered red and orange arrive at the observer's eye. Finally, dust, smoke and water droplets are large particles compared with the wavelength of light, and such particles scatter all wavelengths roughly equally rather than favouring the short ones, so no colour predominates and the sky or the beam appears white or hazy instead of blue.
questions.explanation: The definition must identify scattering as redirection without change of wavelength, and the wavelength dependence must be stated explicitly. Each of the three appearances then needs its own link: blue from molecular scattering, red from the length of the path, and white from large-particle scattering being nearly equal for all colours.
questions.commonMistake: Explaining the blue sky but not the red sunset, or treating the dusty sky as a contradiction. The particle size changes the wavelength dependence, which resolves it.

questions.prompt: Explain why stars twinkle while planets generally do not, identifying the physical process responsible.
questions.answer: The process responsible is atmospheric refraction. Air density, and therefore refractive index, increases downwards through the atmosphere, so light from a star is bent progressively towards the normal on its way to an observer, making the star appear slightly higher than its true position. The atmosphere is constantly moving, with pockets of air at different temperatures and densities passing across the line of sight, so the amount of bending fluctuates from moment to moment; the apparent position of the star therefore wobbles and the amount of light reaching the eye varies, and this flickering is what we see as twinkling. A planet appears as a small disc rather than a point of light, so it sends many slightly different rays through the atmosphere at once, and the fluctuation in one ray is cancelled by that in another, giving a steady average; planets therefore seldom twinkle visibly.
questions.explanation: The answer must name atmospheric refraction rather than scattering, explain the fluctuation in the bending, and then give the disc-against-point argument for planets. Naming the process alone accounts for only part of the marks.
questions.commonMistake: Attributing twinkling to scattering. Twinkling is a refraction effect caused by a fluctuating atmosphere.

questions.prompt: The wavelength of visible light is about 400 nm for violet and 700 nm for red, where one nanometre is one ________ of a metre; the frequency of light of wavelength 500 nm is ________ hertz.
questions.explanation: A nanometre is one billionth of a metre, so 400 nm is 400 billionths of a metre and 700 nm is 700 billionths. Frequency follows from speed equals wavelength times frequency, so f = c divided by the wavelength: 300000000 divided by 500 x 10 to the minus 9 metres gives 3 x 10 to the 8 divided by 5 x 10 to the minus 7, which is 0.6 x 10 to the 15, that is 6 x 10 to the 14 hertz.
questions.commonMistake: Forgetting to convert nanometres to metres before dividing, which gives an answer a billion times too large.

questions.prompt: Which region of the electromagnetic spectrum is used for radar, satellite communication and cooking, and why does it heat food?
options: Infrared, because it is absorbed by the surface of the food
Microwaves, because they make water molecules rotate rapidly
Ultraviolet, because they carry enough energy to break chemical bonds
X-rays, because they penetrate and are absorbed throughout the food
questions.answer: Microwaves, because they make water molecules rotate rapidly
questions.explanation: Microwaves of a few centimetres wavelength penetrate the food and are absorbed by water molecules, which align with the oscillating field and are forced to rotate billions of times a second. The resulting internal friction raises the temperature of the food throughout rather than heating it only at the surface. Infrared heats mainly at the surface, and ultraviolet and X-rays are used for sterilisation and imaging rather than for cooking.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing infrared because it is the familiar radiation of heat. Infrared warms the surface, whereas microwaves heat the interior by molecular rotation.

questions.prompt: Arrange the following in order of increasing frequency, state which has the greatest energy per photon, and give one use and one hazard of each of the two extremes: gamma rays, visible light, microwaves, X-rays.
questions.answer: Frequency is inversely proportional to wavelength because the speed of every electromagnetic wave in a vacuum is the same, so the order of increasing wavelength is the reverse of the order of increasing frequency. The increasing-frequency order is microwaves, then visible light, then X-rays, then gamma rays. Since the energy of a photon is proportional to frequency, gamma rays, having the greatest frequency, carry the greatest energy per photon and are therefore the most penetrating and the most damaging to living tissue. Gamma rays are used to sterilise medical equipment and to treat cancer by destroying tumour cells, and their hazard is severe damage to healthy tissue, so sources must be shielded and doses limited. Visible light is used for sight, photography and optical communication, and its hazard is limited, although an intensely bright source can dazzle or damage the retina.
questions.explanation: The order must be justified from the constant speed linking wavelength and frequency, and the energy argument must be tied to frequency rather than asserted. The two extremes each need a use and a hazard, and the hazard of gamma rays should be connected to their photon energy.
questions.commonMistake: Ordering by wavelength and calling it frequency. The two orders run in opposite directions, which is the point of the question.
